VOTING TRUSTS AND SHAREHOLDER VOTING AGREEMENTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes two devices that California's General Corporation Law recognizes for pooling or delegating how shares get voted: a written voting agreement among shareholders, and a voting trust in which shares are transferred to one or more trustees who vote them. It states the requirements, time limits, and filing obligations that Corporations Code §§ 705 and 706 attach to these arrangements for Acme, Inc., a stock corporation. It does not cover a proxy given for a single meeting or a short period (that is a different, narrower mechanism also addressed in § 705), it does not cover a close corporation's shareholder management agreement that dispenses with a board of directors under Corporations Code § 300(b) (a separate statutory device available only to a corporation that has made the statutory close-corporation election), and it does not cover the mechanics of cumulative voting for directors. This document states facts about what the statute requires and permits; it does not recommend whether Jordan Lee or any other shareholder should enter into a voting trust or voting agreement, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about a specific transaction.

TWO DISTINCT STATUTORY DEVICES FOR CONTROLLING HOW SHARES ARE VOTED
California Corporations Code § 706, part of the General Corporation Law's chapter on "Voting of Shares" (§§ 700–711), recognizes two distinct arrangements by which shareholders can control how their shares are voted, in addition to the ordinary proxy governed by § 705. Under subdivision (a), two or more shareholders can sign a written agreement specifying how their shares will be voted, without transferring the shares to anyone. Under subdivision (b), shareholders can instead transfer their shares by written agreement to one or more trustees, who then hold the right to vote and otherwise represent the shares — a "voting trust." The statute treats these as separate mechanisms with separate formal requirements, and expressly provides that an agreement valid under one need not satisfy the formalities of the other.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "CHAPTER 7. Voting of Shares [700 - 711]"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 706 (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, Chapter 7 (Voting of Shares), heading and section number (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=706.)
  "an agreement between two or more shareholders of a corporation, if in writing and signed by the parties thereto, may provide that in exercising any voting rights the shares held by them shall be voted as provided by the agreement"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 706(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, shareholder voting agreement provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=706.)
  "Shares in any corporation may be transferred by written agreement to trustees in order to confer upon them the right to vote and otherwise represent the shares for such period of time, not exceeding 10 years, as may be specified in the agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 706(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, voting trust provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=706.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the existence and basic structure of the two devices under § 706; it does not state which device, if either, suits a particular set of shareholders, and it does not address how a voting trust or voting agreement interacts with a corporation's existing bylaws, a shareholders' buy-sell agreement, or a close corporation's shareholder management agreement under § 300(b), each of which is a separate statutory or contractual arrangement not analyzed here.

THE SHAREHOLDER VOTING AGREEMENT: NO TRANSFER OF SHARES REQUIRED
A voting agreement under § 706(a) requires only that two or more shareholders sign a written agreement specifying how their shares will be voted — by a fixed rule stated in the agreement, by the shareholders' subsequent mutual agreement, or by a procedure the agreement sets up. The shareholders are not required to transfer their shares to a third party to make the agreement effective, though they may choose to do so. The statute overrides the general contract-law objection that an agreement to vote a certain way should not be specifically enforced because money damages would be an adequate remedy: it states directly that such an agreement cannot be denied specific performance on that ground, or on other grounds relating to a court of equity's jurisdiction.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "the parties may but need not transfer the shares covered by such an agreement to a third party or parties with authority to vote them in accordance with the"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 706(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, terms a shareholder voting agreement may fix (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=706.)
  "Such an agreement shall not be denied specific performance by a court on the ground that the remedy at law is adequate or on other grounds relating to the jurisdiction of a court of equity."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 706(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, specific performance of a shareholder voting agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=706.)
  Known gap: The statute displaces one specific defense to specific performance (adequacy of the legal remedy) and one category of equity-jurisdiction objections; it does not state that every voting agreement will be specifically enforced regardless of other defenses (for example, a defense based on fraud, unconscionability, or a defect in the agreement's formation), and those questions are for a court applying ordinary contract principles.

CREATING A VOTING TRUST: A WRITTEN TRANSFER CAPPED AT 10 YEARS
A voting trust is created when shares are transferred by written agreement to one or more trustees who are thereby given the right to vote and otherwise represent the shares. The period for which a voting trust may run is set by the agreement itself, but the statute caps that period at 10 years. Once created, the trust's validity during that 10-year window is not undercut by the fact that its own terms might be read to let it run longer than 10 years — the statute expressly says so — but this does not mean the trust can lawfully exceed 10 years without using the extension procedure described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Shares in any corporation may be transferred by written agreement to trustees in order to confer upon them the right to vote and otherwise represent the shares for such period of time, not exceeding 10 years, as may be specified in the agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 706(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, voting trust creation and 10-year term cap (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=706.)
  "The validity of a voting trust agreement, otherwise lawful, shall not be affected during a period of 10 years from the date when it was created or last extended as hereinafter provided by the fact that under its terms it will or may last beyond such 10-year period."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 706(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, validity of a voting trust during its initial term (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=706.)
  Known gap: The statute caps the trust's stated term at 10 years and separately protects the trust's validity during that period; it does not itself state what happens to the trustees' voting authority after the 10 years run without a timely extension, or what remedy a beneficiary has if a trustee refuses to vote the shares as the trust agreement directs — those are questions of trust and contract law not answered by the text of § 706 alone.

EXTENDING A VOTING TRUST BEFORE IT EXPIRES
A voting trust can be extended beyond its original (or previously extended) expiration date, but only within a specific window and only by specific parties. The extension must be agreed to within the two years immediately before the trust's then-current expiration date. It requires a written agreement by one or more of the trust's beneficiaries together with the written consent of the voting trustee or trustees. Each extension, like the original trust, is capped at an additional period of not more than 10 years, measured from the expiration date as it stood before that extension.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "At any time within two years prior to the time of expiration of any voting trust agreement as originally fixed or as last extended as provided in this subdivision, one or more beneficiaries under the voting trust agreement may, by written agreement and with the written consent of the voting trustee or trustees, extend the duration of the voting trust agreement with respect to their shares for an additional period not exceeding 10 years from the expiration date of the trust as originally fixed or as last extended as provided in this subdivision."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 706(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, procedure and time window for extending a voting trust (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=706.)
  Known gap: The statute is specific about the two-year window, the need for beneficiary agreement plus trustee consent, and the 10-year cap on each extension, but it does not address what happens if some beneficiaries extend and others do not (the text says the extension operates "with respect to their shares"), and it does not specify a required form for the written consent beyond writing itself.

FILING THE VOTING TRUST AGREEMENT AND THE RIGHT TO INSPECT IT
A duplicate of the voting trust agreement, and of any extension of it, must be filed with the secretary of the corporation whose shares are held in trust. Once filed, that duplicate must be open to inspection by a shareholder, a holder of a voting trust certificate, or the agent of either — on the same terms that apply to inspecting the corporation's record of shareholders. This filing-and-inspection duty applies to voting trusts formed under subdivision (b); it is a separate requirement from the specific-performance rule that applies to voting agreements under subdivision (a).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A duplicate of the voting trust agreement and any extension thereof shall be filed with the secretary of the corporation and shall be open to inspection by a shareholder, a holder of a voting trust certificate or the agent of either, upon the same terms as the record of shareholders of the corporation is open to inspection."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 706(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, voting trust filing and inspection requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=706.)
  Known gap: The statute does not specify a deadline (measured in days) for filing the duplicate after the trust or its extension is created, and it does not state what consequence follows if the corporation's secretary fails to file or make available the duplicate, beyond whatever general remedies the corporation's record-inspection statutes otherwise provide.

A VOTING AGREEMENT DOES NOT HAVE TO SATISFY VOTING-TRUST OR PROXY FORMALITIES
The statute forecloses a specific argument that could otherwise be used to attack a § 706(a) voting agreement: that it should be treated as invalid because it looks like a voting trust that does not comply with subdivision (b)'s formalities, or like a proxy that does not comply with § 705. Subdivision (c) states that an agreement made under subdivision (a) may not be held invalid or unenforceable on either of those grounds. Separately, subdivision (d) confirms that § 706 does not invalidate any other voting or shareholder agreement, or any irrevocable proxy that complies with § 705(e), as long as that agreement or proxy is not otherwise illegal.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No agreement made pursuant to subdivision (a) shall be held to be invalid or unenforceable on the ground that it is a voting trust that does not comply with subdivision (b) or that it is a proxy that does not comply with Section 705."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 706(c) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, voting agreements are not invalidated by voting-trust or proxy formalities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=706.)
  "This section shall not invalidate any voting or other agreement among shareholders or any irrevocable proxy complying with subdivision (e) of Section 705, which agreement or proxy is not otherwise illegal."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 706(d) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, section does not invalidate other shareholder agreements or compliant irrevocable proxies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=706.)
  Known gap: These subdivisions remove two specific grounds for invalidating an agreement (mischaracterization as a noncompliant voting trust or a noncompliant proxy); they do not immunize an agreement from being challenged on other grounds, such as an argument that its subject matter is otherwise illegal or that it was not properly formed under ordinary contract law.

A RELATED BUT SEPARATE DEVICE: THE IRREVOCABLE PROXY TIED TO A § 706 AGREEMENT
Corporations Code § 705 governs proxies generally, and as a default rule a proxy is revocable at will by the person who executed it. Subdivision (e) lists specific categories of proxy holders for whom a proxy can instead be made irrevocable for a stated period, including, as one of six listed categories, "a person designated by or under an agreement under Section 706" — tying an irrevocable proxy to the same voting-agreement mechanism described in this document. Consistent with that link, subdivision (e) also provides that such a proxy becomes revocable once the underlying § 706 agreement has terminated, alongside the other listed events (redemption of a pledge, termination of a purchase option, payment of a secured debt, and so on) that end the other categories of irrevocable proxy.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(5) A person designated by or under an agreement under Section 706."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 705(e)(5) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, irrevocable proxy held by a person designated under a § 706 agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=705.)
  "the agreement under Section 706 has terminated, or the person ceases to be a beneficiary of the trust"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 705(e) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, an irrevocable proxy tied to a § 706 agreement becomes revocable once that agreement terminates (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=705.)
  Known gap: This clause describes how one category of irrevocable proxy under § 705(e)(5) is linked to a § 706 agreement; it does not restate the full list of six categories under which a proxy can be made irrevocable, or the separate rule in § 705(f) that an irrevocable proxy can still be cut off as to a transferee who takes shares without notice of the proxy's existence unless that existence appears on the share certificate or transaction statement.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
By signing below, Jordan Lee acknowledges having received and reviewed this information sheet regarding voting trusts and shareholder voting agreements under California Corporations Code §§ 705 and 706 with respect to Acme, Inc., a stock corporation, and understands that it describes the applicable statutory framework as a factual matter and does not recommend for or against entering into any particular voting trust, voting agreement, or proxy arrangement, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about a specific transaction.

Signed: ___________________________
Jordan Lee

Date: September 1, 2026

City, State: Oakland, California
